title: Transistor Alpha and Beta Explained Simply | PUC Electronics Class 11
description:
Aarav's lab manual says a transistor has a current gain of one hundred. Can one small part really make current a hundred times bigger, and what do alpha and beta mean? A transistor has three legs but a circuit needs two wires in and two out, so one leg is shared: common base, common collector or common emitter, the one used most.

On a live breadboard we build the common emitter circuit (input between base and emitter, output between collector and emitter). A hundred runners leave the emitter: 99 reach the collector and 1 is stuck in the base, so alpha = 99/100 and beta = 99. Then the formulas alpha = IC/IE and beta = IC/IB, and step by step from IE = IB + IC to beta = alpha/(1 - alpha) and alpha = beta/(1 + beta), plus ac beta. The scope draws the input curve (base current shoots up past about 0.7 V, like a diode) and the output curves (flat in the active region, higher for a bigger base current). Worked example: alpha = 0.98 gives beta = 49. Then the exam trap, where it is asked, an original board pattern practice question with a full solution, and a formula card to screenshot.
